content: Nitrocellulose, also known as cellulose nitrate or flash paper, is a highly flammable compound created by nitrating cellulose through exposure to nitric acid or another potent nitrating agent. When used as a propellant or a low-order explosive, it is referred to as guncotton. Uses of Nitrocellulose: 1. Smokeless Gunpowder: Nitrocellulose is a primary component of smokeless gunpowder, which is used in firearms and explosives. 2. Early Photographic Film: It was used in early black-and-white photographic films, particularly before 1948. 3. Western Blotting and DNA Immobilization: Nitrocellulose membranes or paper are utilized in laboratory techniques like Western blotting for immobilizing DNA and proteins due to their non-specific affinity for amino acids. This property is also exploited in diagnostic tests such as pregnancy tests, urinary albumin tests, and C-reactive protein (CRP) tests. 4. Wart Removal: Nitrocellulose is used as a carrier for salicylic acid in products like Compound W Wart Remover. 5. Collodion in Photography: In early photographic emulsions, collodion (a solution of nitrocellulose) was used as a carrier for silver salts, often spread in thin layers on glass plates. 6. Magician’s Flash Paper: Sheets of nitrocellulose paper or cloth are used in magic tricks, as they burn almost instantaneously with a bright flash and leave no ash. 7. Cosmetics and Testing: It is used in nail polish, hair coloring, and radon tests for alpha track etches. 8. Lacquer for Guitars and Aircraft: Nitrocellulose lacquer was widely used as a finish for guitars throughout the 20th century and is still used in some applications today. It was also used as an aircraft dope, applied to fabric-covered aircraft to tighten and protect the material. 9. Secure Disposal in Cryptography: Nitrocellulose has been used as a transportation medium for one-time pads in cryptography, allowing for complete and secure disposal of the pads. Guncotton: In 1832, Henri Braconnot discovered that treating starch or wood fibers with nitric acid produced a lightweight, combustible material called xyloidine. Later, in 1838, Théophile-Jules Pelouze treated paper and cardboard similarly, creating a material he named nitramidine. Both substances were highly unstable and impractical as explosives. In 1846, Christian Friedrich Schönbein, a German-Swiss chemist, accidentally discovered a more practical method for producing guncotton. While working in his kitchen, he spilled concentrated nitric acid and wiped it up with a cotton apron. After drying, the apron exploded. Schönbein’s method involved immersing fine cotton wool in a mixture of sulfuric and nitric acids, washing it in cold water to remove acid residues, and drying it below 100°C. Schönbein collaborated with Rudolf Böttger, who independently discovered the process in the same year. Another chemist, F.J. Otto, also produced guncotton in 1846 and was the first to publish the process. The process uses nitric acid to convert cellulose into cellulose nitrate, with sulfuric acid preventing water from diluting the nitric acid. Guncotton’s power made it suitable for blasting and as a projectile driver, generating six times the gas volume of black powder with less smoke and heat. However, its sensitivity during production led to its discontinuation by the British, Prussians, and French within a year. Jules Verne referenced guncotton optimistically in his novels, such as From the Earth to the Moon, where it was used to launch a projectile into space. Further research revealed that careful preparation of the cotton was crucial to prevent spontaneous explosions. The British, led by Frederick Augustus Abel, developed a longer manufacturing process in 1865, extending washing and drying times to 48 hours and repeating them eight times. The acid mixture was also adjusted to two parts sulfuric acid to one part nitric acid. Guncotton remained useful for limited applications, but a more stable and slower-burning mixture was needed for firearms. This led to the development of smokeless powder. Dissolved guncotton (approximately 25% in acetone) forms a lacquer used in wood finishing to create a hard, lustrous surface. Nitrate Film: Nitrocellulose was the first flexible film base, introduced by Eastman Kodak in August 1889. Camphor was used as a plasticizer for nitrocellulose film. It was used for X-ray films until 1933 and motion picture films until 1951, when it was replaced by safety film with an acetate base. The flammability of nitrate film necessitated fireproof projection rooms with asbestos wall coverings. The U.S. Navy even produced a training film demonstrating the ignition of nitrate film, which continued to burn even when submerged in water. Public safety concerns led to restrictions, such as the London Underground banning nitrate films. Fires caused by nitrate film stock were a significant hazard, as depicted in the Italian film Cinema Paradiso. Today, nitrate film projection is highly regulated, requiring extensive safety measures, including fireproof containment for reels and automatic fire extinguishers aimed at the film gate. These precautions prevent devastating fires but may damage projection equipment. Nitrocellulose film decomposes over time, releasing nitric acid, which accelerates its degradation into a flammable powder or goo. Low temperatures can indefinitely delay this reaction. Most early 20th-century films were lost due to decomposition or studio warehouse fires. Film archivists face significant challenges in preserving old films. Other Uses: Depending on the degree of esterification during manufacturing, nitrocellulose burns at varying rates. Low-esterification nitrocellulose is used in products like tennis balls, guitar picks, and some photographic films, which burn more slowly and leave charred residue. In professional wrestling, nitrocellulose flash paper is used to perform an illegal move called a Fireball, where a wrestler ignites the paper and throws it at an opponent, creating the illusion of a supernatural fireball.
